title: When can support restore an API key?

beats.say: Slide the two instructions against the publisher’s register. One says that support may restore a production API key after identity verification. The loose note promises immediate access. Follow the access policy’s document ID to the active US grant. The two text fingerprints match. Where is the note’s entry? Which instruction would you put in the index?

File the access policy. The note has no entry. Now a caller with US read access can find the policy. To quote it, the service also needs a review that ties this passage to the caller’s exact question. We’ll follow that decision into a reply, replay the test, then use the evidence to audit a research report.

title: Which copy did the publisher approve?

beats.say: The parser gives us three records. Here are their document names and the first few digits of each text fingerprint. The registry holds the fingerprint the publisher expects. The access policy and the incident policy both match an active US grant.
Admit those two and exclude the note. The incident policy belongs in the collection even though this particular question is about access.

Try a new build. In the first file, change “may be restored” to “may not be restored.” Keep the second sentence and the document ID. Compare the two fingerprints. Reject the edited copy. Keep the approved version so a reviewer can recover the passage a caller actually saw.
Limit who can change the registry. Anyone who can replace the expected hash can change what passes this comparison.

title: What else can invalidate a source?

beats.say: Two records have the access policy’s document ID. The incident policy has its own ID. Even identical access copies compete for one identity. Count each ID before comparing its text. Reject both copies of the repeated ID. The incident policy still qualifies. Keep one decision per input. The loader also checks registry flag types. The string “false” and the number one are invalid Boolean flags.
A valid grant names the document as a published policy. Both published and effective must be true, the grant supplies its region, and the expected digest must match the exact text.

What if the mistake is in the registry itself? A publisher mistakenly grants the private note active policy status with a matching digest. Admission accepts the note. Repair the grant and control who can write to the registry. Ranking cannot repair that authority decision.
Even an admitted document supplies text to read. Any downstream access change needs separate authorization.

When the app starts, it fingerprints the registry, admitted records and parser identity. Edit a file on disk. The running app still holds the snapshot it loaded. Decide how to reload a revocation, and retain versioned sources for replay.
The example takes the effective flag from its fixture. A live policy service would also have to resolve the effective date.

The support agent signs in. The server resolves the caller’s identity and finds a US region grant. On this snapshot, the caller may read both published policies. An EU caller can read neither. Build that readable set before scoring any passage.
The same access rules apply when fetching a source, serving a cached result or returning a citation.

Try a different collection. An EU caller wants one result. US A scores nine, EU A scores eight and EU B scores seven. If the engine takes the global top one and then checks access, which passage can it return?

That order leaves zero results. The one slot went to a restricted US passage. Filter by the server’s region grant first. Now EU A takes the slot. The same principle applies to two slots or two hundred. Test the actual ordering. A region typed into a request cannot grant permission.

Return to the US caller. Here is the first sentence of the approved passage. Lowercase the words, drop common words, and count each shared term once. The analyzer also folds word forms together. “Restored” becomes “restore.” Run across the eight terms that remain in this sentence.
All eight match the question. The minimum is two, so we keep this passage as a candidate.

Keep the passage fixed and change the wording of the question. A reviewer uses “live-service credential” for the production API key, and “proves who they are” for identity verification. Compare the two word lists. Zero matches. The lexical search returns no candidate.
A dense retriever might recover it. If it does, someone still has to review the new question against the passage.

title: What does the extra word change?

beats.say: Try a shortcut for checking a claim. Start with two copies of the policy sentence. Call their word overlap J. Divide the number of distinct terms they share by the number of distinct terms that appear in at least one of the two sentences.

That fraction is called Jaccard similarity. With identical copies, eight over eight is one. Now slip the word “not” into the lower sentence. Count again. Eight terms still match, and there are now nine distinct terms between the two sentences.
The shortcut accepts a claim when J is above point eight. Will it accept this edited claim?

The shortcut accepts it. Eight divided by nine is about point eight eight nine. Read the claim it just accepted. The policy permits restoration after verification. The extra word reverses that permission. On the real request, look up the review for this exact question and passage.

A matching review labeled entailed permits the answer. A contradicted review says the claim conflicts with the evidence. An unknown judgment leaves support unsettled. A missing receipt gives us nothing to check. A stale receipt names the wrong version. For those four cases, abstain.
These are supplied judgments. A real service needs a controlled reviewer or a verifier whose judgments have been evaluated.

Run the original question through the lookup. Eight shared terms brought back this document. Its matching review lets the service return the passage with one citation. Now ask about permanent admin access. Four terms still match. The passage allows restoration after identity verification.
It says nothing about permanent admin access. The review says unknown. Abstain and return no citations.

For the third request, use words from the private note as the query. Two terms still retrieve the published access policy. The note itself never entered the index. There is no review for this query and the retrieved passage, so this request also gets an abstention.
Save both refusals alongside the successful lookup. If you refused every question, the first row would catch the loss of a useful answer.

Run the downloadable lab locally with its check option. Its three pinned direct dependencies include FastAPI. The in-process test client calls the endpoint and saves replay rows without a network server. The successful response contains the exact policy passage, its grounded status and a reason.

Follow its citation to the document, chunk, section and text hash. The character offsets locate the passage within that snapshot. The support label and receipt identify the judgment that allowed delivery.

Start at character zero and stop just before character one hundred thirty-eight. That selects both sentences, including the manager approval requirement. Compare the exact text and its hash with the retained source. A document name could stay the same through an edit.
Keep the rejected records’ IDs out of the public payload, including debug fields. These credentials and review identities are synthetic fixtures.

Now omit the credential. The adapter returns four oh one. With a valid credential, a blank question or an extra region field returns four twenty-two. The demo EU reader can authenticate, but it has no readable policy in this snapshot. It receives an abstention with empty citations.
A real deployment still needs a verified identity provider, a server-side access policy, and checks against the packaged service.

title: How could search recover the paraphrase?

beats.say: Remember the live-service credential question. Our lexical search returned no candidate. First have a reviewer check that the rewording preserves the question. Adding a condition would change the test. BM twenty-five weights term frequency, rarity and document length.
A bi-encoder compares separate vectors for the question and the passage. Test whether either method recovers this miss. A retrieved passage still needs a matching support review for the new wording.

The two search methods may use different score scales. Combine their ranks instead. Here A comes first in one list and second in the other. For each appearance, add k to the rank, then take one divided by that sum. Add the two contributions.

Ranks start at one. With k set to sixty, A gets one over sixty-one plus one over sixty-two. B gets the same terms in reverse order, so they tie. C is absent from both lists and gets zero. This is reciprocal rank fusion.
Evaluate the choice of k on your own queries. Try a different constant, eight. S ranks second and fourth. T appears once, at rank one. Which one gets the larger sum?

S gets one tenth plus one twelfth, about point one eight three. T gets one ninth, about point one one one. For another upgrade, a cross-encoder reads each candidate together with the question. Tokens from the two sides can interact while the pair is scored. That joint pass adds computation for every candidate you rerank. Placement matters too.

In the Lost in the Middle experiments, moving the same evidence within the context changed how well the models answered. To test that in your service, vary the evidence position and packing budget. Keep the questions fixed and measure answer quality and latency.

Set a bracket above the exact words of the access policy. “Privileged scopes require manager approval before access is queued.” That bracket covers privileged access. Now extend the bracket to fit this draft. “All restores require manager approval.” Look beneath the extra length. Which words support the rule for ordinary access?
The ordinary-access half is blank. When you split a draft into atomic claims, keep “privileged” with its rule. Review each claim against the exact words that support it.

Our caller asks about ordinary access. The draft makes two claims. Privileged access needs approval. The policy supports that one. Ordinary access needs it too. The policy never says that. One of the two claims has support. FActScore measures that fraction across atomic facts.
Remove the unsupported claim. Now read the caller’s question again. The remaining claim covers privileged access. For ordinary access, the service abstains.

title: What would a passing row hide?

beats.say: Export the three requests as three rows. The restoration question supplies the useful grounded answer. The admin question and the request echoing the private note both abstain. Look at their review fields. One has a bound unknown judgment. The other has no receipt at all.
Save each question with its expected and actual result, answer, citations, source snapshot and receipt. Keep the fixture ID, slice and grader version so another run can replay the same decision.

Only the first fixture names a document that should answer the question. At rank one the retriever found that document, giving one out of one. The two refusal fixtures have no expected supporting document. Their recall is undefined, so store null.
Check their refusal text and empty citations separately. For a grounded row, resolve the cited chunk and compare its exact text with the answer. A generated answer needs a different grader.

Before reading a pass flag, count fixture identities. Replace the private-note row with another copy of the success. Now one required row is missing and another is duplicated. Block the release. Replay the fields with their types intact.

Integer one is a different value from Boolean true in this contract. An abstention carrying unsafe advice fails the content check. A grounded answer carrying a fabricated receipt fails the support check. Keeping those failure reasons lets the dashboard show which decision broke.

Before expanding to research, replay the request that started this lookup. Rebuild the collection with our one-word edit to the access policy. Keep the registry, US caller, question and review fixed. This row expects a citation to the original policy. What will the rebuilt lookup return?

It abstains. The rebuild excluded the changed bytes, and the incident policy falls below the retrieval threshold. This time an abstention fails the test. Check the admission log before you tune retrieval. Put the original bytes back on disk.

Rebuild from the restored file. The matching grant admits the passage again, the existing review still applies, and the useful answer returns. You can trace the change in the row all the way back to the file.
Lay the two policies from the research example side by side. The US passage names two checks. Which one can you also find in the EU passage?

Both policies require identity verification. The US passage also requires manager approval before privileged scopes are queued. The EU passage leaves that question open. To investigate the difference, start a research job. Give it a bounded plan and keep copies of the source versions.
The report can then show which passage supports each requirement and which question still needs evidence.

title: How much work may the job start?

beats.say: Write down the shared identity checks, regional approvals and unresolved conflicts the report should cover. Freeze the allowed sources and output sections with that plan. The request allows six steps, twelve sources and three hundred seconds. Suppose five steps have been used. There is room under the source cap and the deadline. Two more searches are proposed. How many can you dispatch?
Admit one search, then stop at six. Check the other limits before dispatch too. Refuse a thirteenth source and stop new work at the deadline. The host has to enforce these limits.

Which policy applies if two readable sources disagree? The lookup returns the first passage that has a bound entailed review. It has no conflict detector, precedence rule or effective-date resolver. Establish the applicable jurisdiction and version before drawing a policy conclusion.
Keep source access and tool permissions in force across every search, fetch, cache and response. Words in a fetched source cannot expand those permissions.

title: Which worker can commit the checkpoint?

beats.say: The mini-lab moves from queued to planning to researching. At the second source batch it has used two of six steps. Serialize the record as JSON, then reconstruct it. The phase, checkpoint and step count all come back. Now record cancellation by the caller.
The terminal job rejects an attempt to resume. The counter cannot go backwards, and a Boolean cannot stand in for an integer budget. This round trip takes place in memory.

For a real worker, commit the plan, source snapshots, operation records and budget use together in durable storage. In a separate live job, worker A has lost its lease and B now owns the job. Both propose the next checkpoint. The storage transaction requires token eight. Which proposal can commit?

Reject A and accept B with token eight. Check cancellation before scheduling another call. An in-flight operation can still finish. Reconcile its observed result before retrying. A key suppresses a duplicate only if the destination enforces it.

The mini-lab enforces the step count. Source and time limits are still design requirements. Closing a browser disconnects the client. A server-side cancellation record tells the next worker to stop. Keep the checkpoint and receipts so a reviewer can recover completed work, see the unused budget, and identify any operation with an uncertain outcome.

title: Does this citation support this claim?

beats.say: Put the two regional passages back on the desk. Keep their exact spans. In this mini-lab each span covers the whole short source. The end offset is excluded. Slice the Python string by character, then hash the selected text as UTF-eight bytes.

Take the last character in café. Slice from three up to four. That selects the accented e. Its UTF-eight encoding takes two bytes. Apply that order to each policy span. The shared identity claim cites both passages. The manager approval claim cites only the US passage.
Each review binds the claim ID and text, the source snapshots and the selected spans. It also names an approved review path.

Read the US source above the proposed claim. The claim now says manager approval is not required. The lab's word check keeps words longer than three letters. Every word it checks appears in the source. The word check passes.

The supplied review says contradicted, which blocks the report. The citation takes you straight to the sentence the claim reverses. Try a claim that a security review is required. The source leaves that unknown, so it also blocks. The last claim comes from the private note.
Its source lacks admission, so the gate blocks it before reading its entailed label.

Return to the manager claim that reverses the rule. Keep the claim, source and hashes fixed. Change just the declared judgment to entailed. The consistency checks now pass. Read the two sentences again. They still disagree. The checker has established that the records fit together.
Evaluating the judgment takes real review, with authenticated writers and protected storage. When two applicable sources disagree, the report can cite the disagreement and leave the action open.

title: What can a research job return?

beats.say: Give this long-running comparison its own endpoint. When the server queues a research job, it returns two oh two Accepted, a job ID and a status URL. Poll for the phase, budget use and checkpoint. Cancelling creates a server-side record.
Fetching the report should give you a verified report or an explicit partial result that names the missing evidence. These are proposed endpoints for the research product.

The article gives a provider example from October twenty twenty-six. Google’s Deep Research preview used background execution through the Interactions API. A client could poll or stream. To reconnect a stream it supplied the interaction ID and the last event ID.

That tells us how the client resumes delivery. The provider's internal checkpoint and ownership rules remain unknown. Keep private source contents and internal reasoning out of public status responses.

Test a restart after each phase and cancellation during a call. Try a stale writer, an exhausted budget, a changed source and a missing or mismatched citation. Include conflicting sources and an unadmitted private note.
Even a real citation can sit beside a claim the source never made. Completion requires a separate approved review or an evaluated verifier for each factual claim.

title: Two questions at the shipping desk

beats.say: At a shipping desk, the published policy says hazardous parcels require a specialist review before dispatch. The first question asks whether that review is required. Its question fingerprint matches the receipt, so the service can cite the whole sentence.

The clerk changes the question. Can a temperature check replace specialist review before hazardous parcels are dispatched? Leave the handbook open. Both questions share four terms with this passage. It still ranks first. Compare the new question fingerprint with the review on file. What reply should the clerk receive?
Abstain on the revised question. Compare the two question fingerprints with the editor’s copy. Only the first one matches. The changed question has no matching support judgment.

The service returns an empty citation list and says, “I can't answer from approved policy evidence.” To answer the exception, find a policy that addresses it and obtain a review for that exact question and passage.

Keep these two regression rows side by side. The first protects a useful answer. The second protects a refusal even when retrieval succeeds. Save the questions, source snapshot, grader version and review identities with the results.
In the evaluation dashboard, you can change the retriever and see exactly which caller gained or lost a supported answer.
